transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi, yeah—good to meet you too. I guess what finally pushed me to come in is that I’m having a harder time keeping all the moving parts organized. It’s not like everything is falling apart, exactly, but between patent notes, workshop prep, gallery deadlines, and team decisions, I keep finding myself just starting whatever feels loudest in the moment instead of what actually matters most. And that’s been… frustrating. I’m not sure if that’s the right way to explain it.
Did you have similar trouble staying organized and focusing when you were a child?

Yeah… I think so. I mean, I did fine in school overall, so I don’t want to overstate it, but looking back, it was kind of there even in grade school.

Teachers would write things like I was bright but daydreamed a lot, or that I needed to remember to turn things in. I’d finish assignments and then somehow not hand them in, or I’d lose the homework folder before it made it back to school. That was all before I was a teenager, so… yes, I guess it’s not totally new.
Have you ever had a period where you felt unusually up or energized compared with your normal self?

I don’t think so… not in a way that feels unusual, anyway. I mean, I’ve had times where I’m really into a project and I can get a little energized by it, but I wouldn’t say it’s outside my normal range. Unless you mean something more specific?
Are these focus and organization problems causing significant problems for you at work?

Yeah… I mean, I’d like to say it’s mostly just annoying, but honestly it’s starting to show at work in ways I’m not proud of.

I missed a checkpoint for a patent filing, which… wasn’t great. And there was a pretty difficult architecture review where I don’t think I came across as on top of things, and some of the collaborators seemed to be questioning whether I should be leading the larger project. That’s hard to say out loud, because I do care and I’m not trying to be careless. But yes, I think it’s affecting my reputation some.
Do these focus and organization problems also affect you outside of work?

Yeah… I think it does, though I’ve maybe been framing it as “I’m just busy” for a long time.

What finally pushed me to come in is that I can’t seem to keep all the moving parts organized anymore — patent notes, workshop prep, gallery deadlines, team decisions, all of that. I’ll sit down meaning to handle the important thing, and then I end up doing whatever feels most urgent or loudest in the moment, even if it’s not actually what matters most.

I don’t know if that’s the kind of thing you mean, but… yes, it’s not just at work.
Do these focus and organization problems happen in more than one part of your life, not just at work?

Yes… I think so. I don’t want to overstate it, but it’s definitely not only work.

What finally pushed me to come in is that I can’t seem to organize all the moving parts anymore — patent notes, workshop prep, gallery deadlines, team decisions — and I end up starting whatever feels loudest or most urgent instead of what actually matters. If that makes sense.
Do you spend a lot of time worrying, even when there isn’t an immediate problem to solve?

I’m not sure I’d describe it as a lot of worrying, exactly. I mean, I think about things I need to handle, but it doesn’t feel like I’m sitting around worrying when there’s no actual problem.

Maybe I’m splitting hairs a bit… but to me it feels more like trying to keep track of things than being anxious all the time. Is that distinction useful?
Do you often feel a strong need for things to be done in a very specific or exact way?

Not really, I don’t think so. I mean, I like things done well, and I can get particular about some work stuff, but I wouldn’t say I need everything done in one exact way.

If someone has a different way that works, I’m usually fine with that. At least… I think I am. Is that the kind of thing you mean?
Did these problems get noticeably worse after a specific stressful event or major change in your life?

Yes… I think there was a pretty clear shift. I wouldn’t say it was one traumatic event or anything, but after the award, I got pulled into leading a lot more coordination-heavy work.

Since then — maybe about a year and a month now — it’s been more of a real problem. Before that I could kind of compensate, or at least it looked like I was managing. Does that answer what you’re asking?
Before your responsibilities increased last year, were these focus and organization problems already causing noticeable difficulties in your adult life?

Before that, I think it was more… manageable. I’m sure there were some things I had to work around, but I wouldn’t say it was causing major noticeable problems in adult life.

It really became a real problem about a year and a month ago, after the award led to me taking on more coordination-heavy responsibilities. That’s when it started to stand out more. Does that make sense?
Do you often avoid or put off tasks that require sustained mental effort, like paperwork, detailed planning, or long reading?

I’m not completely sure how much I do that. I mean, I don’t think of myself as someone who just refuses those kinds of tasks.

Paperwork and detailed planning aren’t exactly things I look forward to, but I think that’s probably true for a lot of people. I may put them off sometimes if they feel too involved, but I’m not sure I’d call it “often.” Maybe it depends on the task. Does that answer it, or should I be thinking about it in a more specific way?
When your workload is lighter, do these focus and organization problems still interfere with your functioning?

When the workload is lighter, it’s… less obvious, I think. I can usually patch things together better.

But I don’t want to make it sound like it hasn’t mattered. It has started to affect how people see me at work, which is hard to admit. I missed a checkpoint on a patent filing, and there was a really difficult architecture review where I think some collaborators came away questioning whether I could actually lead the larger project.

So maybe it’s not only workload, but the heavier workload makes it much harder to hide. Is that the kind of interference you mean?
Outside of work, do you still have trouble organizing everyday things like bills, appointments, or household tasks?

Outside of work, it’s a little harder for me to pin down. I don’t think I’m, you know, completely unable to manage bills or appointments or anything like that.

But the organizing piece does show up. What really pushed me to come in is that I can’t seem to keep all the moving parts straight anymore—patent notes, workshop prep, gallery deadlines, team decisions—and then I end up starting with whatever feels most urgent or loudest, instead of what actually matters most.

So yes, I guess it’s organization more broadly, not just one task. I’m not sure if that answers the everyday-life part exactly.
If your responsibilities at work went back to what they were before the award, do you think these problems would mostly go away?

I think they’d probably get better, yes. I don’t want to overstate it.

But I’m not sure they’d mostly go away, because this has been a real problem for… about a year and a month now, since the award kind of pushed me into leading more coordination-heavy work. Before that, I could manage things more quietly, I guess.

So if the responsibilities went back, I’d expect it to be less exposed, but I’m not completely sure it would just disappear. Does that make sense?
During times when work is not especially demanding, do you still have trouble deciding what to start and keeping yourself organized?

Yes… I think so. Maybe not as dramatically when work is lighter, but I still do have trouble figuring out what to start with.

It’s like, what finally pushed me to come in is that I can’t seem to keep the moving parts organized anymore—patent notes, workshop prep, gallery deadlines, team decisions—and then I just start with whatever feels loudest or most urgent, not necessarily what actually matters most.

I don’t know if that counts as the same thing when work isn’t especially demanding, but the pattern is still there, I think.
Do you often miss personal appointments?

Not often, I don’t think. I mean, I’m usually pretty careful with appointments because I know it would look bad to miss them.

I may occasionally cut it close or need reminders, but I wouldn’t say I’m regularly missing personal appointments. At least, not that I’ve noticed. Is that the kind of thing you mean?
Do you often find your attention drifting when someone is speaking to you, or while you’re reading?

Yes… that does happen. I wouldn’t say I’m trying not to listen or anything, but in architecture meetings especially, someone will be talking and I’ll catch the first few words, then my mind sort of jumps to some implementation detail.

Then they’ll ask me a direct question and I realize I didn’t actually follow the whole thing, so I have to ask them to repeat it. It’s embarrassing, honestly. I try to cover it by saying I want to make sure I understood, but… yeah, my attention does drift that way sometimes.
Before age 12, did you often have trouble paying attention or staying organized?

I think… yes, looking back, it was there pretty early. I don’t want to overstate it, because I did well in school, but my teachers would write things like that I was bright but daydreamed a lot.

And I remember having finished assignments that I just forgot to turn in, or losing homework folders. That was definitely before I was a teenager. I guess at the time it got framed as me being a little scattered rather than a real problem, if that makes sense.
As a child, did these attention or organization problems cause trouble for you at home?

At home… I’m not totally sure how much trouble it caused, honestly. I don’t remember it being, like, a major crisis or anything.

I’m sure my parents probably reminded me about things or got frustrated sometimes, but I don’t have a clear memory of it causing big problems at home. Maybe I was just seen as kind of forgetful or needing nudges. Is that helpful, or are you asking more about consequences like arguments or punishments?
Before age 12, did these attention or organization problems also happen at school, not just at home?

Yes, I think it did show up at school too. Not in a dramatic way, I guess, because I was still considered a good student… but looking back, the comments were there.

Teachers would write that I was bright but daydreamed, and I remember forgetting to turn in assignments that I had actually finished. I also lost homework folders more than once. That was all in grade school, definitely before I was 12.

I hope that answers what you mean—school was probably where it was most noticeable, even if people framed it pretty gently at the time.

patient.answer:
At home… I’m not totally sure how much trouble it caused, honestly. I don’t remember it being, like, a major crisis or anything.

patient.answer:
Yes, I think it did show up at school too. Not in a dramatic way, I guess, because I was still considered a good student… but looking back, the comments were there.

Teachers would write that I was bright but daydreamed, and I remember forgetting to turn in assignments that I had actually finished. I also lost homework folders more than once. That was all in grade school, definitely before I was 12.
